{"concepts_used":["GC-0001","GC-0002","GC-0009","GC-0010","GC-0011","GC-0017","GC-0019","GC-0038","GC-0168"],"decline_reason":"","declined":false,"citations":[{"ref":"TMM/Part29/2/2/2","quote":"A connotation may result from the whole trade mark or from a part of the trade mark. It may result from a dictionary meaning or from a connection in the minds of the buying public with some person, place or thing."},{"ref":"TMM/Part29/9/9/3~1","quote":"Qualifiers (e.g. “made in”, “product of”) are not necessary for a connotation to be present in a mark."},{"ref":"TMM/Part29/9/9/3~1","quote":"A trade mark containing a standalone geographical reference will cause confusion if each of the following criteria are met: Consumers would have reason to associate the goods/services with the geographical location; The association between the place and the goods/services would influence the purchasing decision of an average consumer of the goods/services. There are no other elements in the mark, or surrounding circumstances, which would mitigate the risk of confusion."},{"ref":"TMM/Part29/9/9/3~2","quote":"Although the trade mark contains a reference to Tuscany, the word EFFECT changes the connotation of the trade mark. Consumers are not likely to think the paint originates from Tuscany, but rather that the paint will give a surface a Tuscan-style finish."},{"ref":"TMA1995/s43","quote":"An application for the registration of a trade mark in respect of particular goods or services must be rejected if, because of some connotation that the trade mark or a sign contained in the trade mark has, the use of the trade mark in relation to those goods or services would be likely to deceive or cause confusion."}],"answer":"**Who is affected? — Manual practice:** The relevant people are the buying public for the goods or services. A place reference can create an association in their minds; the Manual asks whether that association would influence an average consumer’s purchasing decision. [TMM/Part29/2/2/2; TMM/Part29/9/9/3~1]

**What changes in shoppers’ perceptions? — Manual practice:** The reference can suggest geographical origin, even without words such as “made in”. But the rest of the mark can change that suggestion. In the Manual’s TUSCAN EFFECT paint example, consumers are described as expecting a Tuscan-style finish, rather than paint originating in Tuscany. This illustrates the difference between an origin message and a style or appearance message. [TMM/Part29/9/9/3~1; TMM/Part29/9/9/3~2]

**When does confusion matter? — Manual practice:** For a standalone geographical reference, the Manual requires a reason to associate the goods or services with the place, an influence on purchasing decisions, and no other mark elements or surrounding circumstances mitigating the risk of confusion. A place reference alone therefore does not establish that risk under this guidance. [TMM/Part29/9/9/3~1]

**Legal rule — Act:** Section 43 requires rejection where a connotation of the mark, or a sign within it, makes use for the particular goods or services likely to deceive or cause confusion. That is the statutory rule; the Tuscany example is Manual guidance, not a prediction about a particular application. [TMA1995/s43; TMM/Part29/9/9/3~2]"}
